problem.statement_vernacular: Knee pain on the right side

subjective.vernacular: Where exactly in the knee does it hurt, and how would you describe the pain — sharp, aching, burning, or something else?
subjective.why_it_matters: Medial versus lateral versus diffuse pain, and character such as aching versus sharp versus burning, helps distinguish osteoarthritis from meniscal tear, ligamentous injury, or referred pain.

subjective.vernacular: When did the knee pain start, and did it come on gradually or suddenly?
subjective.why_it_matters: Gradual insidious onset over months to years favors osteoarthritis or chronic overuse, while sudden onset suggests acute injury such as meniscal tear or ligament rupture.

subjective.vernacular: What makes the pain worse — stairs, prolonged sitting, twisting, or walking — and what makes it better?
subjective.why_it_matters: Pain worse with weight-bearing and activity relieved by rest is characteristic of osteoarthritis, while pain at rest or at night raises concern for inflammatory arthritis, infection, or neoplasm.

subjective.vernacular: When you wake up, is the knee stiff, and if so how long does that stiffness last before it loosens up?
subjective.why_it_matters: Morning stiffness lasting less than 30 minutes supports osteoarthritis, whereas stiffness lasting more than 45–60 minutes suggests inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis.

subjective.vernacular: Does the knee ever lock up, catch, click, or give way unexpectedly?
subjective.why_it_matters: Locking or true catching suggests a loose body or meniscal tear, while giving way indicates possible ligamentous instability or patellofemoral dysfunction.

subjective.vernacular: Has the knee been visibly swollen, and if so does swelling come on quickly after injury or gradually over hours?
subjective.why_it_matters: Rapid hemarthrosis within hours of injury points to ligamentous tear or fracture, while slow effusion developing over 24 hours is more consistent with meniscal injury or inflammatory arthritis.

subjective.vernacular: Have you ever injured this knee before, had surgery on it, or been told you had a torn ligament or cartilage?
subjective.why_it_matters: Prior ACL tear, meniscectomy, or intra-articular fracture significantly increases lifetime risk of post-traumatic osteoarthritis in the affected knee.

subjective.vernacular: Do you have pain, swelling, or stiffness in other joints, skin rashes, eye problems, or mouth sores?
subjective.why_it_matters: Polyarticular involvement, rashes, uveitis, or oral ulcers raise the possibility of rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis, or other systemic inflammatory conditions.

subjective.vernacular: Have you ever been told you have gout or crystal deposits in a joint, or had sudden attacks of intense joint pain and redness that resolved on their own?
subjective.why_it_matters: A history of crystalline arthropathy or classic acute attacks makes gout or calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease a candidate explanation for episodic knee pain.

subjective.vernacular: How far can you walk before the pain stops you, and what daily activities — like getting up from a chair, climbing stairs, or dressing — have become difficult?
subjective.why_it_matters: Quantifying functional limitation establishes severity baseline and guides whether conservative care, rehabilitation, or surgical referral is most appropriate.

subjective.vernacular: Have you had fever, unexpected weight loss, night sweats, or fatigue alongside the knee pain?
subjective.why_it_matters: Constitutional symptoms accompanying joint pain raise concern for septic arthritis, systemic inflammatory disease, or malignancy involving bone or synovium.

subjective.term: Body weight and recent weight change
subjective.vernacular: What is your current weight, and have you gained or lost significant weight recently?
subjective.why_it_matters: Obesity is a major modifiable risk factor for knee osteoarthritis progression, and recent weight gain can accelerate joint loading symptoms.

objective.term: Standing alignment — varus or valgus deformity
objective.vernacular: Assessment of whether the knee bows outward (bow-legged) or inward (knock-kneed) when standing

objective.term: Range of motion — active and passive
objective.vernacular: How far the knee can bend and straighten, both on the patient's own effort and when the examiner moves it
Fluid swelling inside the knee joint detected by palpation or ballottement of the patella

objective.term: Joint line tenderness — medial and lateral
objective.vernacular: Whether pressing along the inner or outer joint line reproduces pain
Special maneuvers that stress the meniscus to see if they reproduce a click or pain

objective.term: Ligamentous stability testing (Lachman, anterior/posterior drawer, varus/valgus stress)
objective.vernacular: Examiner tests whether the knee moves abnormally in ways that suggest torn ligaments

objective.term: Patellofemoral provocation (Clarke sign, patellar grind, patellar apprehension)
objective.vernacular: Tests that press or move the kneecap to see if it causes pain or a grinding sensation

objective.term: Weight-bearing plain radiographs of right knee — AP, lateral, and sunrise views
objective.vernacular: Standard X-rays of the knee taken while standing to assess joint space, bone spurs, and alignment
Calculated weight-to-height ratio used to assess obesity as a contributing factor
Blood test measuring uric acid level to evaluate for gout
Blood markers of inflammation that rise with inflammatory arthritis or infection
Blood tests that help identify rheumatoid arthritis

objective.term: Synovial fluid analysis — if effusion present
objective.vernacular: Lab examination of fluid drawn from inside the knee joint, looking at cell count, crystals, and culture

assessment_candidates.vernacular: Wear-and-tear breakdown of the knee joint cartilage that develops over time
not_yet_testable: s-002 (onset and duration — not yet gathered)
o-002 (range of motion — not yet examined)
assessment_candidates.basis: Osteoarthritis is the most prevalent cause of knee pain in adults over 45; characterized by gradual onset, activity-related pain, crepitus, bony enlargement, and radiographic joint space narrowing with osteophytes.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: No record data exist yet; probability reflects strong population prior for knee pain in general adult presentation labeled probable OA.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Without management, joint damage and functional loss can progress and become difficult to reverse, ultimately requiring joint replacement.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: A tear in the rubbery cartilage pads (menisci) that cushion the knee
not_yet_testable: o-004 (joint line tenderness — not yet examined)
assessment_candidates.basis: Meniscal tears are common causes of knee pain at all ages; degenerative tears are particularly prevalent over age 40 and may coexist with or be mistaken for osteoarthritis.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Cannot distinguish from OA without physical exam maneuvers and imaging; probability held conservatively pending workup.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: An untreated symptomatic tear can cause persistent pain, swelling, and accelerate cartilage loss if a displaced fragment causes mechanical damage.

assessment_candidates.term: Crystalline arthropathy — gout or calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD)
assessment_candidates.vernacular: Joint pain caused by uric acid crystals (gout) or calcium crystals (pseudogout) depositing inside the knee
not_yet_testable: o-010 (serum uric acid — not yet ordered)
o-013 (synovial fluid analysis — not yet performed)
assessment_candidates.basis: Gout and CPPD can present with acute or chronic knee pain and swelling; CPPD is particularly common in the knee of older adults and can mimic OA on X-ray with chondrocalcinosis.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Cannot rule in or out without serum uric acid, synovial fluid analysis, and targeted history; included because it is treatable and commonly missed.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Recurrent crystal attacks damage joint cartilage over time and cause significant pain episodes; gout is fully manageable with the right treatment.

assessment_candidates.term: Inflammatory arthritis — rheumatoid or seronegative spondyloarthropathy
assessment_candidates.vernacular: An immune system attack on the knee joint lining, as seen in rheumatoid arthritis or related conditions
assessment_candidates.basis: Inflammatory arthritides can present as monoarticular knee involvement; missing this diagnosis leads to progressive joint destruction that is preventable with DMARDs.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Probability is low for isolated knee presentation but rises substantially if prolonged morning stiffness, bilateral involvement, or elevated inflammatory markers are found.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Untreated inflammatory arthritis causes irreversible joint erosion and disability that may not be recoverable even with later treatment.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: Pain originating from the kneecap and its underlying cartilage, often felt at the front of the knee
not_yet_testable: s-003 (aggravating factors such as stair climbing — not yet gathered)
o-007 (patellar provocation tests — not yet performed)
assessment_candidates.basis: Patellofemoral syndrome is a common diagnosis across a wide age range; characterized by anterior knee pain worsened by stairs, squatting, and prolonged sitting.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Cannot assess without knowing pain location and patellar exam; probability will shift substantially once location is clarified.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Generally not destructive but causes significant functional limitation; responds well to targeted physical therapy when identified correctly.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: A bacterial or other microbial infection inside the knee joint requiring urgent treatment
not_yet_testable: s-011 (fever and constitutional symptoms — not yet gathered)
o-013 (synovial fluid analysis — not yet performed)
assessment_candidates.basis: Septic arthritis is uncommon in chronic knee pain but must not be missed; risk rises with recent joint injection, prosthetic joint, immunosuppression, or skin breakdown near joint.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Listed because the consequence of missing it is catastrophic; probability considered very low for a chronic pain presentation but cannot be formally excluded without key data.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Untreated septic arthritis destroys the joint within days and can be fatal from systemic sepsis; it is a medical emergency.

assessment_candidates.term: Bone tumor or metastatic disease involving distal femur or proximal tibia
assessment_candidates.vernacular: A tumor growing in the bone near the knee, either originating there or spreading from cancer elsewhere
not_yet_testable: s-003 (rest pain or night pain — not yet gathered)
assessment_candidates.basis: Malignant bone lesions near the knee can mimic arthritis; rest pain, night pain, and constitutional symptoms are red-flag features; plain X-ray is first screening tool.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Rare in the absence of known malignancy but severity mandates inclusion; probability will drop sharply if X-ray shows only degenerative changes.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: A missed bone malignancy is potentially fatal; early identification changes prognosis dramatically.

residual.vernacular: Something not on this list — the differential is never closed

plan_options.term: Weight-bearing knee radiographs — AP, lateral, sunrise views
plan_options.vernacular: Standing X-rays of the right knee to look for joint space narrowing, bone spurs, and alignment
plan_options.basis: ACR/AAFP guidelines recommend weight-bearing plain films as the first imaging study for suspected knee osteoarthritis; Kellgren-Lawrence grading guides management.

plan_options.term: Structured physiotherapy referral with quadriceps and hip strengthening program
plan_options.vernacular: Referral to physical therapy focused on strengthening the muscles around the knee to reduce joint load
plan_options.basis: OARSI and NICE guidelines rank exercise therapy as first-line treatment for knee OA with strong evidence for pain reduction and functional improvement.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician; carried out by physical therapist

plan_options.vernacular: Guidance and support to reduce body weight to lower mechanical load on the knee
plan_options.basis: Each kilogram of weight loss reduces knee joint compressive force by approximately 4 kg; weight loss combined with exercise is the most effective conservative intervention for knee OA.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician, dietitian, obesity medicine specialist

plan_options.term: Analgesic trial — acetaminophen or topical NSAID first line
plan_options.vernacular: A trial of pain relievers, starting with acetaminophen or a gel/cream NSAID applied to the knee
plan_options.basis: OARSI 2019 guidelines recommend topical NSAIDs as first-line pharmacotherapy for knee OA; oral NSAIDs are effective but carry GI and cardiovascular risk requiring individual assessment.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician; patient can self-initiate OTC acetaminophen

plan_options.term: MRI of right knee — if meniscal tear suspected after exam
plan_options.vernacular: An MRI scan of the knee to look for meniscal tears, ligament injuries, and cartilage damage if physical exam raises suspicion
plan_options.basis: MRI is the gold standard for soft tissue knee pathology with sensitivity >90% for meniscal tears; indicated when clinical exam findings suggest tear that would alter management.

plan_options.term: Serum uric acid and synovial fluid aspiration for crystal analysis
plan_options.vernacular: Blood test for uric acid level and, if fluid is present, drawing fluid from the knee joint to look for crystals under the microscope
plan_options.basis: Synovial fluid analysis is the definitive test for crystalline arthropathy; serum uric acid provides supporting evidence; both are necessary to distinguish gout from CPPD.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician for blood test; physician or trained clinician for joint aspiration

plan_options.term: Inflammatory arthritis serologies — ESR, CRP, RF, anti-CCP
plan_options.vernacular: Blood tests to screen for rheumatoid arthritis and measure the degree of inflammation in the body
plan_options.basis: Anti-CCP has >95% specificity for rheumatoid arthritis; elevated CRP/ESR in the context of prolonged morning stiffness and polyarthritis should prompt rheumatology referral.

plan_options.term: Urgent joint aspiration with synovial fluid Gram stain, culture, and cell count — if septic arthritis suspected
plan_options.vernacular: Emergency drawing of fluid from the knee joint to look for infection if fever, warmth, and rapid onset swelling are present
plan_options.basis: Septic arthritis requires same-day joint aspiration for definitive diagnosis and immediate antibiotic therapy; delay increases risk of irreversible joint destruction and systemic sepsis.
plan_options.who_can_act: Emergency physician or orthopedic surgeon — urgent referral

plan_options.term: Orthopedic surgery referral for consideration of intra-articular corticosteroid injection or surgical options
plan_options.vernacular: Referral to a joint specialist if conservative measures fail, to discuss steroid injections into the knee or surgery such as joint replacement
plan_options.basis: Intra-articular corticosteroid injection provides short-term pain relief in knee OA; total knee arthroplasty is indicated for severe OA with functional limitation refractory to conservative care.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician initiates referral; orthopedic surgeon performs
